common_name: Love-Lies-Bleeding Amaranth (Classic Long Trailing Red Tassel Amaranth)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Love-Lies-Bleeding produces long, drooping, rope-like tassels of tiny deep red flowers that can trail two feet or more, a dramatic, old-fashioned cottage garden and cut-flower favorite.

directions: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has warmed; overly rich soil produces excess foliage at the expense of the dramatic flower tassels. Love-Lies-Bleeding is a long-cultivated ornamental amaranth grown for its striking, long, rope-like, drooping tassels of deep crimson-red tiny flowers that can cascade two feet or more from the top of the plant, an eye-catching, old-fashioned cottage garden focal point and a favorite for both fresh and dried arrangements. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and self-seeds readily in a favorable spot, sometimes becoming a welcome volunteer in following years. Harvest the flower tassels for drying just as they reach full color, hanging them upside down in a cool, dry, dark spot.

common_name: Joseph's Coat Amaranth (Multicolor Foliage Ornamental Amaranth)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Joseph's Coat is grown for its brilliantly multicolored foliage, splashed with red, gold, green, and bronze, rather than for showy flowers.

directions: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has warmed. Joseph's Coat is grown chiefly as a dramatic foliage plant, its upper leaves splashed and blotched in vivid combinations of red, gold, orange, green, and bronze that intensify with heat and full sun, providing bold color through the entire summer without needing showy flowers. It makes a striking specimen or background planting in a hot, sunny border and tolerates drought and poor soil well once established. Young leaves of this species are also edible and used as a cooked green in parts of Asia and Africa, though the plant is most commonly grown in Western gardens purely for its colorful ornamental foliage.

common_name: Century Celosia (Tall Vigorous Plumed Cutting Celosia Series)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Century is a tall, vigorous plumed celosia series bred for long, sturdy stems well suited to cutting, unlike shorter bedding-type celosia.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes. Century is a tall-growing plumed celosia series bred specifically for the cut-flower trade, producing long, sturdy stems topped by dense, feathery flame-shaped plumes in vivid gold, orange, red, and pink that hold their color and form exceptionally well both fresh and dried. Its greater height compared to compact bedding celosia varieties makes it far more practical for cutting gardens and floral arrangements, and the plants tolerate heat and humidity well through a long summer bloom season. Harvest stems for fresh use anytime, or cut for drying once the plumes are fully colored and hang upside down in a dry, dark, well-ventilated spot.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers
